title: Old Fathom

pages.text:
The mudflats stretched out like a giant’s abandoned breakfast. Grey and wet, it smelled of rot and old fish guts. Juno squinted through the rain, her yellow raincoat bright against the gloom. Beside her, Teo adjusted his round glasses, wiping the water from his messy black hair. He kept one hand on his tool belt, even though there was nothing to fix here.

"Where are we going?" Teo asked, his voice tight. "This isn’t a place for shoes. Or dignity."

Barnacle scuttled across a piece of driftwood, his chipped blue teapot shell bobbing. "Honestly! It’s a mudflat. It’s where things go when they’re tired of being alive. Or useful. You know how it is."

Juno ignored him. She was looking at the horizon. There, a dark shape lay half-buried in the silt. It was huge. It looked like a boulder with a face.

"Is that a rock?" Teo asked.

"No," Juno said. Her heart gave a strange thump. "It’s a turtle."

Teo blinked. "A turtle. Like a pet shop turtle?"

"Bigger," Juno said.

She pointed. The shape shifted. A long, mossy head rose from the mud. Two eyes, ancient and kind, blinked slowly at them.

"Oh, dear," Barnacle muttered. "That’s Old Fathom. He’s been down here since the tide stopped. He’s dry. He’s sad. He’s also enormous. Try not to step on him."

Juno knelt in the wet muck. The turtle’s skin was rough, like tree bark. He looked at her, and a low rumble started deep in his chest. It vibrated through the mud and into her knees.
pages.image: A small hermit crab in a chipped blue teapot shell stands on a piece of driftwood, gesturing dramatically toward a massive, moss-covered sea turtle emerging from grey mud, with a girl in a yellow raincoat and a boy in a green cap watching in the background.

pages.text:
The turtle’s voice was like the sound of a cello being played underwater. Deep, slow, and warm.

"The water... is gone," the turtle rumbled. "The breath... is stopped."

"Hello," Juno said, trying to keep her voice steady. "We’re Juno. This is Teo. And this is Barnacle, who is being rude."

Barnacle hissed. "I am being honest!"

Old Fathom’s eyes closed for a long moment. When he opened them, they were misty. "Ivy... she came here. In the green boat. She poured the water from her bucket. She said, 'Fathom, you must stay wet for the dance to begin.'"

Juno looked at Teo. "He’s thirsty. And he’s stuck."

Teo’s face went pale. "I don’t swim well. I can’t go in the water. I can’t save a turtle that’s the size of a van."

"We don’t need to swim," Juno said. She looked around the muddy shore. "We need buckets. Lots of buckets."

"Buckets," Barnacle repeated. "You want to fill a turtle the size of a house with water. Using buckets. This is the most insane plan I have ever heard. I approve."

Juno stood up. "Teo, you know Mrs. Marchetti, right? Your mom?"

Teo nodded, looking terrified. "Yes."

"Go get her. Tell her we need the whole bakery. Every bucket, every jug, every mop. Tell her it’s an emergency."

"An emergency?" Teo squeaked. "They’ll ask questions!"

"Tell them the tide is sick," Juno said. "And that I’m a doctor."

"Barnacle, can you talk to the seagulls?"

Barnacle puffed out his little chest. "I can talk to many things. But the seagulls are busy stealing shiny things. However..." He looked at Teo. "If you promise not to laugh at me, I will try."

Teo looked at the giant turtle, then at Juno. He took a deep breath. "Okay. I’ll go. But if I get mud on my shoes, I’m blaming you."
pages.image: A giant sea turtle with moss on its shell lies stranded in grey mud, looking up at a girl in a yellow raincoat and a boy in a green cap, while a small hermit crab in a blue teapot shell stands nearby on a rock.

pages.text:
Within ten minutes, the bakery doors burst open. Mrs. Marchetti stood there, flour on her apron, holding a broom. Behind her was a line of staff, customers, and a confused delivery driver.

"What is going on?" Mrs. Marchetti demanded.

"Emergency," Juno said, not blinking. "Turtle. Thirsty. Big."

Mrs. Marchetti looked at the turtle. Then at Juno. Then at Teo, who was hiding behind a bucket.

"He’s my friend’s client," Teo said weakly.

Mrs. Marchetti sighed. She looked at Old Fathom. The turtle blinked at her. Something in her eyes softened. She dropped the broom. "Everyone! Buckets! Now!"

It started with a trickle. Then a stream. The staff of the bakery, wearing their white coats, marched to the edge of the mudflats. They carried buckets, jugs, and even a large silver tea urn.

Juno joined them. She carried a small bucket, filling it from a nearby puddle. She poured it over the turtle’s shell. The water hissed as it hit the dry skin. Old Fathom let out a long, shuddering sigh.

Teo stood back, arms crossed. He watched a baker named Marco pour water from a fire extinguisher. It was not water, but it was wet.

"This is ridiculous," Teo said. "We are watering a rock."

"He’s not a rock," Juno said, though her arms were tired. "He’s a friend."

Barnacle was on a high spot, directing traffic. "More water on the left! No, the other left! You’re going to give him an earache!"

Mrs. Marchetti looked at Juno. "You’re a strange girl, Juno Vale."

"I’m a Tide Keeper," Juno said, though she kept her voice low.

"Of course you are," Mrs. Marchetti said. She picked up another bucket. "Now stand back. We have a job to do."

The mud was slippery. Juno slipped, catching herself on the rim of a bucket. Her raincoat got muddy. She didn’t care. The turtle was waking up. His eyes were brighter. His shell was glistening.
pages.image: A group of bakery staff in white coats and aprons carry buckets and jugs of water toward a giant sea turtle on the mudflats, while a girl in a yellow raincoat pours water from a small bucket, her face determined.

pages.text:
The turtle’s skin was no longer dry. It was slick and dark. He stretched his long neck, and the sound was like a deep groan of relief.

"Thank you," he rumbled. "The water... it tastes of salt and kindness."

"Kindness?" Teo asked, stepping forward. "We just poured tap water on you."

"Not just tap water," Old Fathom said. He looked at Juno. "I remember when the tide was young. I remember when the first Keeper climbed the lighthouse. She had a whistle like a spiral shell. She listened. The sea answered."

Juno felt a warmth in her chest. "Grandma Ivy?"

"She was the last," Old Fathom said. "But the sea remembers. It waits for the next voice. The voice that listens, not the one that shouts."

Juno looked at Barnacle. The crab was silent for once. He looked down at his teapot shell.

"Ivy was my friend," Barnacle said softly. "She used to bring me crumbs. I complained, but I liked it."

Old Fathom shifted his weight. The mud squelched. "You need the Moon Pearl. It is in the wreck of the Dolly Marigold."

Juno frowned. "Where is that?"

"Where the tide goes to sleep," Old Fathom said. "Look for what the moon keeps. It is in the mud. It waits for the one who hums."

Teo scratched his head. "That’s a riddle. I hate riddles. They’re just puzzles with no instructions."

"It’s not a riddle," Juno said. "It’s a map."

Barnacle crawled over to her. "The Dolly Marigold sank fifty years ago. It’s a pile of rust and barnacles. You’ll need a map. Or a very good guess."

Juno looked at the log in her bag. She thought of Grandma Ivy’s handwriting. *Where the tide goes to sleep.*

She looked at the mud. It was grey and still. It looked like sleep.

"We go now," she said.

Teo groaned. "It’s raining. And I have shoes."

"You have a tool belt," Juno said. "You can fix anything. Even your fear."

Teo looked at her. For a second, he looked afraid. Not of the water, but of being the one to fail. Then he straightened his green cap.

"Fine. But if I get stuck, you’re pulling me out."
pages.image: A giant sea turtle with moss on its shell looks up at a girl in a yellow raincoat and a boy in a green cap, while a small hermit crab in a blue teapot shell stands on a rock, listening intently.

pages.text:
They walked toward the darker part of the bay. The rain had stopped, but the air was thick with mist. The mud was deeper here. It sucked at their boots.

Teo tried to keep his feet dry. He failed. Mud splashed onto his green cap. He looked like a swamp creature.

"Barnacle," Teo said, "do you have a map?"

Barnacle was on his shoulder. "I have a memory. And a grudge. The Dolly Marigold was owned by a man who stole my favorite seagull. I remember the hull. It has a hole in the side."

"A hole?" Juno asked.

"A big one," Barnacle said. "It’s where the pearl sleeps. Or hides. Pearls are sneaky."

Juno looked at the horizon. The lighthouse was a dark silhouette. The Dolly Marigold should be nearby.

They walked for an hour. The mud got thicker. Teo’s boots squelched with every step. He was miserable.

"I’m going to die in this mud," he muttered.

"You’re not," Juno said. "You’re just wet."

"Wet and dying."

Barnacle yawned. "Honestly, the drama is exhausting."

Juno stopped. She looked at the water. It was calm now. The mist was lifting. And there, in the distance, she saw it. A dark shape. A broken mast. The wreck of the Dolly Marigold.

"There," Juno whispered.

Teo looked. "That looks like a skeleton."

"It’s a ship," Juno said. "And it’s waiting for us."

She took a deep breath. The air smelled of salt and old wood. She felt a pull, gentle but strong. Like a hand reaching out from the water.

"Ready?" she asked.

Teo wiped mud from his glasses. "No. But I’m here."

Juno smiled. She reached into her pocket and took the spiral shell whistle. She didn’t blow it. She just held it. She listened.

The sea was quiet. But it was listening back.
pages.image: A girl in a yellow raincoat and a boy in a green cap stand in thick grey mud, looking toward a dark, broken shipwreck in the distance, while a small hermit crab in a blue teapot shell sits on the boy's shoulder.

summary: Juno, Teo, and Barnacle rescue the stranded sea turtle Old Fathom by enlisting the help of the entire bakery to pour water on him. Old Fathom reveals that the Moon Pearl is hidden in the wreck of the Dolly Marigold, a ship that sank fifty years ago. The group walks to the wreck, with Teo struggling with the mud and his fear, but Juno senses the sea is listening to her.
